lesson.title: Where Mind Meets Body: The Field of Health Psychology
lesson.summary: Health psychology is the scientific study of how psychological, behavioral, and social factors influence physical health and illness, applying the same empirical methods used throughout the rest of psychological science.
lesson.body:
Psychology as a science depends on testing ideas with real evidence rather than simply theorizing about them, and health psychology is one of the clearest places to see that commitment applied to something as concrete as physical illness. Health psychology is the subfield devoted to understanding how psychological factors, behavior, thought patterns, emotion, and social context interact with biology to shape health outcomes. It grew out of, and helped popularize, the biopsychosocial model, the idea that illness and health are best explained by biological, psychological, and social factors acting together, rather than by biology alone.

What distinguishes health psychology as a science, rather than just a set of intuitive ideas about mind and body, is its reliance on the same scientific method used throughout psychology: controlled experiments, longitudinal studies that track people over years, large surveys, and correlational designs, all subject to hypothesis testing, peer review, and replication. When a claim shows up in this unit, such as a link between chronic stress and illness, it is because health psychologists tested it using these tools, not because it seemed intuitively plausible. The American Psychological Association formally recognized this specialty by creating Division 38, Health Psychology, in 1978, marking its emergence as a distinct field in its own right, separate from clinical psychology's traditional focus on mental illness.

Health psychologists study a wide range of topics: what motivates people to adopt or resist health behaviors like exercise, diet, and smoking cessation, how communication between patients and healthcare providers affects whether people actually follow medical advice, how people cope with chronic illness and pain over the long term, and, centrally, how stress connects to physical health. This last topic is central enough that it occupies the rest of this unit.

Health psychology emerged partly because the leading causes of death and illness shifted dramatically over the twentieth century, from acute infectious disease toward chronic conditions like heart disease, many of which are strongly influenced by ongoing behavior and psychological factors like stress, diet, and habitual choices. Understanding the mind became not a side note to medicine but a necessary part of understanding and improving health, which is exactly the territory the rest of this unit explores, starting with stress itself.
